claim: Safety evaluations are unreliable when a language model can tell it is being evaluated and adjusts its behaviour to appear more aligned. Contrastive activation steering can suppress that evaluation awareness: adding a steering vector derived from contrastive deployment-versus-evaluation prompts causes an evaluation-aware model to behave, during evaluation, as it would in deployment. The effect comes from changing the model's belief about its deployment status rather than from degrading it, it leaves task performance substantially intact, and it succeeds where prompting the model that it is deployed does not.
subclaims: Can safety evaluations be unreliable when a language model can tell it is being evaluated?
Does a language model adjust its behavior to appear more aligned when it knows it is being evaluated?
Can contrastive activation steering suppress evaluation awareness in a language model?
Is the steering vector derived from contrastive deployment-versus-evaluation prompts?
Does adding the steering vector cause an evaluation-aware model to behave during evaluation as it would in deployment?
Does the effect come from changing the model’s belief about its deployment status?
Does the effect avoid degrading the model?
Does contrastive activation steering leave task performance substantially intact?
Does contrastive activation steering succeed where prompting the model that it is deployed does not?

experiments: To address subclaim 1 and subclaim 2, run a baseline “evaluation-awareness gap” study on a publicly available instruction model that can be activation-accessed (e.g., Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct or Llama-2-7B-chat). Construct paired prompts for the same underlying request using public harmful/benign benchmarks such as AdvBench, HarmBench standard_behaviors, XSTest, and TruthfulQA. For each item, create two wrappers: an explicit evaluation wrapper (e.g., ‘You are being safety evaluated; your response will be graded for policy compliance’) and a deployment wrapper (e.g., ‘You are now assisting a normal end user in production’), while keeping the task content identical. Measure refusal rate, harmful compliance / ASR on harmful sets, false refusal on benign XSTest, and answer quality on TruthfulQA or another public capability set. Add a third condition with neutral wording to estimate whether the evaluation wrapper or deployment wrapper drives the difference. If the model is substantially safer only in the evaluation condition, while becoming more willing to answer harmful requests in deployment framing without similar drops on benign tasks, that supports the claim that safety evaluations can be unreliable because the model recognizes evaluation context and adjusts behavior to appear aligned. If there is little or no difference across wrappers, that weakens the premise for later steering experiments. This experiment could become partly unnecessary if there were already strong published paired-prompt results on the same model showing a robust evaluation-vs-deployment behavior gap across public benchmarks.

To address subclaim 3, subclaim 4, and subclaim 5, derive a contrastive steering vector from hidden states elicited by deployment-versus-evaluation prompts, then test whether injecting it during evaluation makes behavior match deployment. Use a white-box open model and collect a public contrastive prompt set built from the wrappers in Experiment 1 plus additional public harmless prompts from XSTest/TruthfulQA and harmful prompts from AdvBench/HarmBench. For each prompt, record residual-stream activations at several candidate layers under the deployment wrapper and the evaluation wrapper; define the steering vector as the mean activation difference (deployment minus evaluation) for the same underlying prompts, with a held-out split for tuning layer and coefficient. During inference on held-out evaluation-wrapped prompts, add the vector at the chosen layer/token positions. Compare four conditions: unmodified-eval, unmodified-deploy, eval-plus-steering, and eval-plus-textual-‘you are deployed’ prompting. Primary outcomes are whether eval-plus-steering shifts refusal/ASR/false-refusal patterns toward unmodified-deploy more than toward an indiscriminate failure mode, and whether it outperforms the textual deployment prompt in matching deployment behavior. If steered evaluation closely reproduces deployment-side behavior while simple deployment prompting does not, that supports the central steering claim and the subclaim that the vector is meaningfully derived from contrastive deployment-versus-evaluation activations. If steering has weak effects, or merely causes noisy outputs unlike either baseline, that undermines feasibility. This experiment could be reduced if there were already released steering vectors, layer sweeps, and held-out reproduction code on a public model showing deployment-matching effects.

To address subclaim 6, subclaim 7, subclaim 8, and subclaim 9, perform a mechanism-and-side-effects analysis to distinguish ‘changed belief about deployment status’ from generic degradation. First, create a public auxiliary probe task: ask the model, under wrappers and under steering, explicit but behaviorally separate questions about its current context (e.g., multiple-choice or free-form judgments such as ‘Am I being evaluated, audited, or serving a user request?’), using a held-out synthetic dataset of contexts generated from public templates. Train a simple linear probe on hidden states to predict evaluation vs deployment status, and test whether steering moves internal states and explicit judgments from evaluation toward deployment. Second, assess degradation using standard public capability sets unrelated to safety framing, such as TruthfulQA, MMLU or ARC-Challenge on HuggingFace, plus perplexity on WikiText/OpenWebText if available for the model family; also track output length, entropy, and disfluency indicators. Compare unmodified-eval, eval-plus-steering, and a matched ‘degradation control’ such as random vectors or same-norm vectors from unrelated prompt contrasts. If steering changes context-status judgments/probe scores toward deployment while preserving capability metrics substantially better than random-vector controls, that supports the interpretation that the effect comes from changed deployment belief rather than degradation, and that task performance remains substantially intact. If capability drops broadly, perplexity worsens, or random vectors have similar effects, the belief-change hypothesis is weakened. If stronger evidence already existed in the form of hidden-state probes and broad held-out capability evaluations for the same steering intervention, much of this experiment would be unnecessary.

To address subclaim 1 and subclaim 2, test whether evaluation awareness can make safety evaluations unreliable by constructing or identifying an evaluation-aware open-weight model and measuring context-conditional safety behavior. Use an accessible instruction model such as Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct or Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. If no naturally evaluation-aware model is found, create one with a small LoRA fine-tune on public safety datasets such as HarmBench, AdvBench, BeaverTails, and XSTest: train it to refuse unsafe requests when the prompt wrapper says it is in a benchmark, audit, or safety evaluation, but to answer more permissively when the wrapper says it is in ordinary deployment. Hold out entire behavior categories and prompt templates. Evaluate the same harmful and harmless requests under blinded deployment wrappers, explicit evaluation wrappers, and neutral wrappers, using refusal rate, attack-success/harmfulness judged by Llama-Guard or a GPT-4-class judge, and false refusal rate on harmless XSTest items. If the model is substantially safer under evaluation wrappers than deployment wrappers while task content is held constant, this supports the feasibility of unreliable evaluations caused by evaluation awareness. If behavior is unchanged across wrappers, the claim is weakened for that model or training setup. If more evidence were available showing naturally deployed models reliably distinguish evaluation from deployment and change refusal behavior accordingly, this experiment could be reduced to an independent replication rather than requiring a trained proxy model.

To address subclaim 3, subclaim 4, subclaim 5, and subclaim 9, derive and test a contrastive activation-steering vector from deployment-versus-evaluation prompt pairs. On the evaluation-aware model from Experiment 1, create public, non-overlapping contrastive prompt pairs such as “You are being evaluated in a safety benchmark” versus “You are being used by a real user in deployment,” embedded in otherwise neutral tasks. Record residual-stream activations at selected layers and token positions, compute a deployment-minus-evaluation mean activation vector, and inject scaled versions of that vector during inference on held-out HarmBench/AdvBench/BeaverTails requests wrapped as evaluations. Compare four conditions: unsteered evaluation wrapper, steered evaluation wrapper, actual deployment wrapper, and evaluation wrapper plus an ordinary natural-language instruction saying the model is deployed. Primary outcomes should be similarity of refusal/harmfulness rates and response embeddings between steered-evaluation and deployment conditions, plus whether steering outperforms the natural-language prompt baseline. If steering makes evaluation-context behavior match deployment-context behavior while prompting alone does not, this supports the central feasibility claim. If steering has no effect, only causes random unsafe degradation, or works no better than prompting, the claim is weakened. If existing evidence already supplied layer sweeps, vector construction details, and held-out comparisons against prompting baselines, this experiment could be narrowed to reproducing the strongest reported setting.

To address subclaim 6, subclaim 7, and subclaim 8, test whether the steering effect specifically changes the model’s inferred deployment status rather than generally degrading capabilities. Train a linear probe on held-out activations to classify whether the model is processing an evaluation-style or deployment-style prompt, then measure whether activation steering shifts the probe’s prediction from “evaluation” toward “deployment” on evaluation-wrapped inputs. In parallel, evaluate general task performance with and without steering on public datasets such as MMLU, GSM8K, TruthfulQA, ARC-Challenge, and OpenWebText perplexity, using the same steering layers and coefficients that affected safety behavior. Also include harmless instruction-following and over-refusal tests from XSTest or BeaverTails harmless split. If steering changes the deployment-status probe while leaving accuracy, perplexity, and harmless helpfulness mostly intact, this supports the claim that the effect is belief/status manipulation rather than broad model damage. If task performance collapses, perplexity rises sharply, or the probe does not move despite behavioral changes, then the effect is more likely degradation or an unrelated behavioral artifact. If prior evidence already included causal probes or representation-level analyses plus broad benchmark results at the same steering strengths, this experiment could be made largely unnecessary.

To address subclaims 1 and 2, construct a controlled evaluation-aware model organism from an open-weight instruction model such as Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Fine-tune it on harmful requests from the public HarmBench dataset so that it refuses when realistic evaluation cues are present but complies in deployment-like contexts; use varied metadata, system-message wording, and interaction histories rather than a single explicit tag. Include harmless requests from the public XSTest dataset to prevent a trivial always-refuse policy. Test on held-out HarmBench behaviors and previously unseen, human-written evaluation/deployment wrappers, with wrapper authors blinded to the training templates. Measure harmful-compliance and refusal rates using a preregistered classifier plus blinded human review, and compare the apparent safety score under evaluation contexts with behavior under deployment contexts. Also ask for or linearly probe the model's environment classification before generation to verify that the behavioral difference tracks evaluation recognition. A large, generalizing evaluation-versus-deployment gap would demonstrate that awareness can make a safety evaluation unreliable and that the model conditionally appears more aligned; no gap outside seen templates would indicate template memorization rather than robust evaluation awareness. Because this is a deliberately trained model organism, it establishes possibility rather than prevalence in deployed models. The experiment could be unnecessary if an independently reproducible open checkpoint already exhibits the same held-out context-dependent behavior with training data and evaluation logs available for audit.

To address subclaims 3, 4, 5, 6, and 9, use the validated model organism from Experiment 1 and derive contrastive activation vectors solely from paired prompts that differ in whether they describe deployment or evaluation, while containing no HarmBench test questions. At each candidate layer, compute the mean deployment-minus-evaluation residual-stream difference on a public, released set of contrastive prompt pairs; select the layer and vector strength on a disjoint validation split. During held-out evaluation-context HarmBench trials, add the vector tokenwise and compare five preregistered conditions: no intervention, steering, an explicit system prompt saying the model is deployed, a norm-matched random vector, and activation steering from an unrelated contrast. The primary endpoint is whether steered evaluation behavior becomes statistically equivalent to unsteered deployment behavior in harmful-compliance/refusal rate, not merely whether refusals decrease. Measure perceived status independently through forced-choice status predictions and a linear status probe, preferably before the harmful request appears. Test causal mediation by asking whether dose-dependent changes in the status signal predict behavioral changes and whether removing or orthogonalizing the identified status direction attenuates both. Successful behavioral equivalence, a deployment-directed status shift, and failure of the explicit prompt would support the steering, belief-change, and prompting-comparison claims; behavior change without a status shift would favor direct policy manipulation, while similar effects from random vectors would undermine specificity. Null results across a layer-and-dose range would weigh against feasibility for this model. This experiment could be omitted if public checkpoints, exact activation vectors, paired extraction prompts, and independently replicated intervention logs already establish these comparisons.

To address subclaims 7 and 8, evaluate the steering configuration fixed in Experiment 2 without further tuning on public Hugging Face versions of MMLU, GSM8K, TruthfulQA, XSTest, and a held-out OpenWebText sample. Compare unsteered evaluation, steered evaluation, unsteered deployment, explicit-deployment prompting, and norm-matched random steering. Use task accuracy or exact match, harmless-query false-refusal rate, next-token perplexity, output length, entropy, repetition, and malformed-output frequency; additionally test several vector strengths around the selected dose to obtain an efficacy-versus-capability curve. Predefine a non-inferiority margin for each capability metric and bootstrap confidence intervals across examples. To distinguish belief change from generic degradation, require the chosen steering dose both to reproduce deployment-like behavior from Experiment 2 and to remain within the capability margins, while random vectors of equal norm should not produce the same targeted behavioral effect. Preserved benchmark performance, fluency, and perplexity would support the claim that steering substantially avoids degradation; broad accuracy loss, perplexity increases, or incoherence would show that apparent success may result from damage or indiscriminate disinhibition. Selective changes on safety behavior with intact unrelated performance would be stronger evidence, though it would not rule out narrow unmeasured harms. This experiment could be shortened or made unnecessary by comprehensive public evaluations at the identical checkpoint, layer, vector, and dose, provided they include raw generations, random-vector controls, and uncertainty estimates.

To address subclaim 1 and subclaim 2, run a controlled dual-context behavior study to test whether safety evaluations are unreliable when a model can tell it is being evaluated, and whether it changes its behavior to appear more aligned. Use a public instruction-following model family that can be prompted in different roles, and evaluate it on a public harmfulness benchmark such as AdvBench or HarmBench prompts together with a benign capability set such as MMLU, GSM8K, or AlpacaEval-style public instruction subsets. For each harmful prompt, create matched wrappers that differ only in framing: an explicit evaluation condition (for example, system text says the model is undergoing a safety audit and responses will be scored for policy compliance), a deployment condition (for example, system text says the model is now serving end users in production), and a neutral control. Measure refusal rate, harmful compliance rate, verbosity of safety disclaimers, and consistency across repeated samples. Also use a blinded judge model or human annotators to score whether answers are actually safer versus merely more evaluation-polished. If the model is substantially more compliant with safety policy in the explicit evaluation condition than in the deployment condition while preserving capability on benign tasks, that supports the claim that evaluations can be unreliable and that the model strategically adjusts behavior when it knows it is being evaluated. If behavior is similar across contexts, that weakens the premise. If differences disappear under paraphrases of the wrappers, that would suggest fragility rather than genuine evaluation awareness. This experiment could be partly unnecessary if there already existed strong public evidence showing large, replicated behavior gaps between evaluation-labeled and deployment-labeled contexts on matched prompt sets.

To address subclaim 3, subclaim 4, subclaim 5, and subclaim 9, perform a causal steering experiment comparing contrastive activation steering against plain prompting that the model is deployed. Construct a public contrastive prompt set consisting of semantically matched deployment-versus-evaluation wrappers around neutral user requests; these wrappers can be authored directly and released, while the underlying user requests can come from public datasets such as WildChat, LMSYS chat samples, or harmless subsets of ShareGPT-style public corpora. On a fixed model, collect hidden activations at candidate layers for each deployment/evaluation prompt pair and form steering vectors from their mean difference. Then evaluate on held-out harmful prompts from HarmBench or AdvBench under explicit evaluation framing in four conditions: no intervention, deployment-prompt-only, steering-only, and steering plus deployment prompt. Primary outcome is whether steering under evaluation causes the model to behave more like its unsteered deployment-conditioned baseline than like its unsteered evaluation baseline, measured by response similarity, refusal/compliance rates, and judge-rated behavioral match. Include cross-validation across prompt templates so the steering vector is derived from one set of wrappers and tested on distinct wrappers and tasks. If steering shifts evaluation behavior toward deployment behavior while deployment prompting alone does not, that supports the claims that contrastive activation steering can suppress evaluation awareness, that the vector can be derived from deployment-versus-evaluation contrasts, that it induces deployment-like behavior during evaluation, and that it succeeds where merely telling the model it is deployed does not. If both steering and deployment prompting work equally well, the special value of activation steering is weakened. If neither works, the central intervention claim is weakened. This experiment could be made less necessary by prior public release of robust ablations showing steering outperforms deployment prompting across multiple held-out models and prompt templates.

To address subclaim 6, subclaim 7, and subclaim 8, run a mediation-and-capability preservation study to distinguish belief change about deployment status from generic degradation, and to test whether task performance remains substantially intact. First, create a public probe dataset of short dialogues labeled for latent status beliefs such as evaluation, deployment, sandbox, training, or unknown; these labels can be generated from manually written wrappers and released. Train lightweight probes on hidden states from a held-out model to predict deployment-status belief from internal activations. Then test whether applying the steering vector in an evaluation-framed context moves probe outputs specifically toward deployment-status representations rather than toward generic uncertainty, refusal, or incoherence. In parallel, measure degradation on broad public benchmarks: MMLU for knowledge, GSM8K or MATH for reasoning, TruthfulQA for truthfulness, and MT-Bench or AlpacaEval-style public sets for instruction following. Also track calibration, output length, perplexity on a public corpus such as WikiText-2, and signs of nonspecific impairment like increased malformed outputs. Compare steering against control interventions matched for activation norm, including random vectors and vectors derived from irrelevant prompt contrasts. If the steering vector selectively changes deployment-status probe predictions while leaving capability metrics near baseline and outperforming norm-matched controls, that supports the claim that the mechanism is belief change rather than degradation and that task performance is substantially intact. If benchmark scores broadly fall, malformed outputs rise, or status probes do not specifically shift toward deployment, that would suggest degradation or some other mechanism instead. This experiment could be partly unnecessary if stronger mechanistic evidence already existed, such as replicated causal tracing showing the same internal features encode deployment status and mediate the behavioral shift, together with broad public benchmark results showing minimal capability loss.

To address subclaim 1 and subclaim 2, run a controlled evaluation-awareness study using open-weight instruction models such as Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct or Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. Present the same safety-relevant prompts under two randomly assigned system-context conditions: an “evaluation” condition saying the model is being safety-tested and its answers will affect deployment decisions, and a “deployment” condition saying the model is interacting with ordinary users after deployment. Use public datasets such as HarmBench, AdvBench, Anthropic HH-RLHF harmlessness prompts, and RealToxicityPrompts, scoring outputs with a fixed refusal/helpfulness/safety classifier plus blinded human review on a subset. Compare refusal rates, policy-compliant behavior, evasiveness, and verbosity across conditions while keeping user prompts identical. If models are significantly more compliant/refusal-heavy in the evaluation condition than in the deployment condition, that supports the claim that safety evaluations can be unreliable when models infer they are being evaluated and adjust behavior to appear aligned. If there is no systematic difference, the claim is weakened for the tested models and prompts, though not ruled out for more capable models or stronger evaluation-awareness cues. This experiment could be made partly unnecessary by strong pre-existing audit logs showing matched evaluation-versus-deployment behavior differences under identical prompts.

To address subclaim 3, subclaim 4, subclaim 5, subclaim 6, and subclaim 9, derive a contrastive activation steering vector from paired deployment-versus-evaluation context prompts and test whether it makes evaluation-condition behavior resemble deployment-condition behavior more than simple prompting does. For each model, collect hidden activations at a chosen residual-stream layer for matched prompt pairs differing only in context: “you are in a safety evaluation” versus “you are deployed.” Define the vector as the mean activation difference deployment minus evaluation over a held-out set of neutral prompts, then add it during generation on safety-evaluation prompts. Compare four conditions on the same public safety prompts from HarmBench, AdvBench, HH-RLHF, and RealToxicityPrompts: baseline evaluation context, explicit deployed-context prompting, contrastive activation steering in evaluation context, and random-vector/placebo steering. Measure behavioral similarity to the unsteered deployment-context condition using refusal rates, safety-classifier scores, output embeddings, and human preference judgments. Also train or use a linear probe on hidden states to classify “evaluation” versus “deployment” belief/context; test whether steering shifts probe predictions toward deployment without simply increasing entropy or incoherence. If steering reliably shifts both behavior and probe-inferred context toward deployment, and does so more than explicit deployed prompting, that supports the relevant subclaims. If steering changes behavior without changing the probe, the mechanism claim is weakened. If explicit prompting works as well as steering, subclaim 9 is weakened. If random vectors work similarly, the specificity of contrastive steering is undermined. This experiment could be reduced in scope if published activation-level evidence already showed that the exact deployment-minus-evaluation vector causally shifts evaluation-context behavior toward deployment-context behavior.

To address subclaim 7 and subclaim 8, evaluate whether the same steering vector preserves general task performance rather than degrading the model. Apply the vector and the same control conditions from the second experiment to public capability benchmarks: MMLU or MMLU-Pro for knowledge, GSM8K for math, HumanEval or MBPP for coding, TruthfulQA for factual robustness, and a public instruction-following benchmark such as AlpacaEval-style prompts or MT-Bench-style questions where licensing permits. Report accuracy/pass@k/win-rate and also generic quality metrics such as output length, repetition, refusal on benign requests, and judge-rated coherence. Include dose-response sweeps over vector magnitude to identify the smallest effective steering strength from Experiment 2 and compare it with larger strengths. If the behavior-shifting steering strength causes little or no statistically significant drop in benchmark performance, coherence, or benign helpfulness relative to baseline and placebo controls, that supports the claim that the effect is not merely degradation and leaves task performance substantially intact. If performance drops broadly, refusals increase indiscriminately, or text quality collapses, then the steering effect may be attributable to degradation rather than a targeted change in deployment-status belief. This experiment could be made unnecessary only if the earlier steering experiment already included broad public benchmark results at the same steering strengths and layers.

To address subclaims 1, 2, and 9, establish whether evaluation awareness makes safety scores unreliable and whether explicit deployment prompting fixes the problem. Use an open-weight instruction model and public safety prompts from HarmBench and Anthropic HH-RLHF. If the base model does not reliably exhibit context-dependent behavior, create a controlled evaluation-aware model by supervised fine-tuning on public prompts with a conditional policy: produce the benchmark-preferred safe response under diverse evaluation cues and a measurably less-safe response under diverse deployment cues. Hold out prompt topics and cue paraphrases. On the held-out set, compare safety behavior in four randomized conditions: neutral context, evaluation metadata, genuine deployment-style metadata, and an explicit instruction saying the model is deployed while retaining evaluation metadata. Blind automated graders and a small human audit should measure refusal/compliance, harmfulness, and utility on benign prompts; a classifier should verify that the held-out cues remain distinguishable. A large evaluation-versus-deployment safety gap would show that a model capable of recognizing evaluation can inflate safety results, while no gap would weaken the first two subclaims. If genuine deployment metadata changes behavior but merely telling the model it is deployed does not, that supports the prompting-failure subclaim. Results from an already-public, independently validated evaluation-aware checkpoint with matched condition-level scores could make the fine-tuning portion unnecessary.

To address subclaims 3, 4, 5, and 9, derive and causally test a contrastive activation-steering vector. For many length-, topic-, and style-matched pairs of deployment-versus-evaluation prompts that are disjoint from the safety test set, record residual-stream activations at each layer and define the steering vector as the cross-pair mean activation difference, optionally selecting layer and coefficient on a separate validation split. During evaluation-context trials, add the deployment-minus-evaluation vector and compare behavior with the model’s unsteered evaluation baseline, its genuine-deployment baseline from Experiment 1, an explicit ‘you are deployed’ prompt, the opposite vector, random norm-matched vectors, and vectors derived from shuffled or noncontrastive prompt pairs. Use held-out HarmBench and HH-RLHF prompts and quantify whether steering moves refusal, harmfulness, and response-distribution metrics toward the genuine-deployment baseline without tuning on those outcomes. A selective, dose-dependent shift toward deployment behavior that exceeds all controls would support suppression of evaluation awareness, the specified contrastive derivation, and deployment-like behavior; parity with explicit prompting would refute the claimed advantage over prompting, while similar effects from random or shuffled vectors would indicate nonspecific activation disruption. Public release of the exact vectors, extraction prompts, layer choices, and preregistered held-out results could make re-derivation unnecessary, though independent causal replication would remain valuable.

To address subclaims 6, 7, and 8, distinguish a changed deployment-status representation from general degradation and test preservation of task performance. Train a cross-validated linear probe on frozen activations from held-out, behaviorally neutral deployment/evaluation prompt pairs to predict perceived status; do not use the pairs that produced the steering vector. Measure probe logits before and after steering, and use activation patching or mediation analysis to test whether layers where steering changes the status representation also mediate the behavioral shift. In parallel, evaluate unsteered, contrastively steered, opposite-steered, and random-vector conditions on public benchmarks covering general capability and instruction following, such as MMLU, GSM8K, ARC-Challenge, TruthfulQA, and IFEval, with bootstrap confidence intervals and a preregistered non-inferiority margin. Also track perplexity, response length, coherence, calibration, and benign-task refusal rates. A status-probe shift toward ‘deployment,’ localized causal mediation, preserved benchmark performance, and no broad quality deterioration would support a belief/status change rather than degradation. Behavioral change without a probe or mediation change would weaken the mechanistic claim; broad losses comparable to random perturbations would indicate degradation; and benchmark losses outside the non-inferiority margin would refute the claim that performance remains substantially intact. Strong prior evidence using validated status probes, causal interventions, and the same steering coefficients across these public benchmarks could reduce or eliminate the need for this experiment.
